AutoCompact

AutoCompact: Learning
When to Compact Context
in Long-Horizon
Coding Agents

First published: July 13, 2026 · Last update: July 15, 2026 · 7 min read

TL;DR

For agentic models, longer context makes it harder to stay oriented throughout the task.

In a coding agent trajectory, the active context accumulates failed greps, irrelevant file reads, reverted edits, and hypotheses the agent has already abandoned. Although most of this history no longer helps, it still sits in the model’s working state and adds noise.

AutoCompact augments the agent’s action space with compact(), allowing the model to decide when to compact its context. Specifically, at natural transition points in the task, when earlier details no longer need to be carried forward, the model can invoke compact() to compress the accumulated history into a summary for the next step, and then continue from there.

Using only 379 SWE-ReBench tasks, we collected 1,052 SFT examples for cold-start training, then further optimized the model with GRPO. Evaluated on SWE-bench Verified, AutoCompact-Qwen3 30B Coder improves over the Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct baseline:

  • Average context-processing cost drops by 15.4%.
  • Across token-budget ranges, the absolute pass rate increases by 10.2% on average, with a maximum improvement of 14.3%.
Instead of remembering more, AutoCompact learns when to compact its context, what to drop, and how to carry the remaining state forward.

Why coding agents need
context compaction

AutoCompact starts from a simple but important observation: if we separate out the key steps that directly contribute to completing the task, much of the remaining work is exploratory. During localization, for example, the agent may inspect several files, compare plausible locations, and test different hypotheses before identifying where the change should be made. These steps are often necessary in the current phase, even if they do not directly appear in the final solution.

But once the agent moves to the next phase, those details may no longer help. What matters is the conclusion it produced, not every intermediate step that led there. Keeping the full exploration in context adds noise. For example, it may cause the model to revisit discarded hypotheses.

This raises the central question: can the model determine when the full history of its prior work is no longer needed and compact its context accordingly? This is not just cutting off old content. The model needs to keep the working state needed for the next step: which paths have been ruled out, which files have been changed, and what needs to be verified next.

AutoCompact learns this transition from the full trajectory to a compact working state for the next phase.

The core idea behind AutoCompact

Figure 1. When the model decides that the current context should be cleaned up, it calls compact() to trigger compaction. After that, the model only sees the initial task, the most recent turns, and the compacted # Auto Context Summary, instead of the full history.

Figure 1 shows the core mechanism of AutoCompact. Most of the time, the model still works like a normal agent: it reads files, edits code, and runs verification. At an appropriate transition point, such as after localizing the issue and before beginning the edit, the model can proactively invoke compact().

When compact() is invoked, the runtime compacts the current context into a # Auto Context Summary. The summary preserves the working state needed for the next phase, while intermediate exploration details are removed from the active context. The model then continues with "original task + recent turns + summary."

Cold-start SFT data: collecting compact behavior in real rollouts

Figure 2. During data collection, the judge checks the original agent actions in the TUI step by step, and corrects key branches into effective trajectories for SFT. At inference time, the judge is removed; the trained agent decides when to call compact() by itself.

AutoCompact requires the model to learn three capabilities: when to invoke compact(), what information to preserve in the summary, and how to continue from the compacted context. Existing models do not reliably exhibit these behaviors. As shown in Figure 2, we therefore introduce a judge model during data collection. Using only the history visible at the current step, the judge reviews each action proposed by the base model.

If the proposed action is already appropriate, the judge leaves it unchanged and advances to the next step. When the judge identifies an appropriate phase transition, it can instead replace the model’s proposed action with compact(). If the resulting # Auto Context Summary omits or misrepresents state needed for the next phase, the judge revises the summary. It can also correct the continuation if the model fails to use the compacted context, such as by repeating exploration that has already been resolved or losing track of conclusions preserved in the summary.

The judge does not rewrite the trajectory arbitrarily. It follows an annotation protocol that specifies valid compaction points, the state each summary should preserve, and the corrections that may be applied. SFT is then performed on the resulting corrected trajectories. At inference time, the judge is removed, and the trained model decides when to invoke compact() and continues from the compacted context on its own.

Using 379 SWE-ReBench tasks and GPT-5.5-Codex as the judge, we collect 1,052 cold-start SFT examples after filtering malformed requests, summary loops, and off-track continuations.

Beyond SFT: Refining
AutoCompact with GRPO

The SFT stage provides a cold start for the basic compaction behavior, but it only teaches the model to imitate judge-corrected trajectories. It does not directly optimize whether a compaction decision ultimately helps solve the task.

Starting from the SFT checkpoint, we continue training with GRPO on SWE-Gym tasks. For each task, we assign a binary outcome reward based on whether the final patch passes the test suite. Because compact() and the post-summary continuation are part of the same trajectory, this outcome reward provides an end-to-end training signal for when to compact, what state to preserve, and how to continue afterward.

Experiment: can AutoCompact
solve more tasks
under the
same context budget?

Figure 3. Submit-at-budget performance under 16k and 256k automatic compaction thresholds. The x-axis shows the cumulative context-processing budget (prompt + output tokens) per task.

For evaluation, we compare AutoCompact-Qwen3 30B Coder (SFT) and AutoCompact-Qwen3 30B Coder (SFT+GRPO) against Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct on SWE-bench Verified under identical scaffold and runtime settings. We test 16k and 256k automatic compaction thresholds. All models use rule-based compaction at the threshold, while the AutoCompact variants can also invoke compact() proactively. We measure submit-at-budget performance by stopping each run at fixed cumulative prompt + output token budgets and evaluating the current workspace patch.

Figure 3 shows that across both compaction thresholds: 1) AutoCompact consistently solves more tasks than the baseline under the same context-processing budget. On average, the SFT model raises the absolute pass rate by 2.6%, while the SFT+GRPO model raises it by 10.2%; 2) AutoCompact uses the available context-processing budget more efficiently: to achieve the same pass rate, the baseline requires a larger token budget; and 3) the compaction policy benefits from outcome-based optimization. GRPO builds on the SFT cold start and delivers a further 7.7% absolute pass-rate improvement over the SFT-only model.

Trajectory analysis:
what did AutoCompact learn?

Trajectory analysis suggests that AutoCompact learns what to preserve more reliably than when to compact. After SFT, the model proactively invokes compact() in 44.3% of tasks; after GRPO, this rises to 58.5%, indicating that outcome-based optimization encourages more active context management. The generated summaries remain highly informative: 99.8% retain relevant task and workspace state, and 97.8% specify a next action. However, many summaries are still triggered during verification, suggesting that learning when compaction is most useful remains an important direction for improvement.
